### What is AI?

Artificial Intelligence is the branch of computer science focused on building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human

Deep Learning (DL)
A specialised subset of ML built on multi-layer neural networks for
large, complex datasets. It excels at image recognition, speech
processing, and anomaly detection in cybersecurity.

# AI and Cybersecurity

## Page 10

### Advanced expert-system components

ATP — Advanced Threat Protection
ATP platforms prevent, detect, and respond to sophisticated
cyber threats by combining several security layers in one
system.
They ingest network, identity, endpoint, and email telemetry —
then apply machine learning to spot patterns that traditional tools
miss.
Examples: Microsoft Defender, CrowdStrike Falcon, and
specialised next-gen XDR platforms.
Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA)
A security model that assumes no user or device is trustworthy
by default. Every access request is continuously verified —
identity, device posture, and context.
Widely used in network and identity stacks: Cisco Zero Trust,
Palo Alto Prisma Access, Okta Identity Cloud.
In 2026, ZTA increasingly extends to AI: agents and tools
authenticate with the same scrutiny as users.

# AI and Cybersecurity

## Page 15

### Potential biases in AI algorithms

What is bias in AI?
AI bias occurs when algorithms make decisions influenced by
prejudice or incomplete data. It can come from:
- Skewed training datasets
- Implicit human bias during model development
- Narrow perspectives in AI design teams
Impact
- False positives / negatives — legitimate activity flagged or
real threats missed
- Discrimination — biometric systems denying access to
certain groups
Mitigating bias
1. Diverse, representative datasets
Avoid skew at the source — sample widely, document gaps.
2. Regular algorithm audits
Run ongoing fairness reviews after deployment, not just before.
3. Human oversight
Keep a human in the loop for high-stakes decisions. Note: the
human's own assumptions matter.
4. Transparent decision logs
Make every model decision auditable so disputes can be reviewed.

## Page 16

### Adversarial attacks on AI systems

Deliberate attempts to deceive or manipulate AI models by exploiting their vulnerabilities. They undermine integrity, reliability, and trust.
Evasion
Inputs crafted to push a model to
the wrong decision (adversarial
examples).
Poisoning
Malicious data injected during
training to teach the model
wrong behaviour.
Model inversion
Reconstructing sensitive training
data from the model's
responses.
Model stealing
Repeated queries used to clone
the model's behaviour into an
unauthorised copy.
Prevention
Adversarial training
Expose the model to attack examples during training so it learns to resist
them.
Data sanitisation
Verify, clean, and version training data before it lands in the pipeline.
Input validation
Filter inbound prompts and content — flag injection patterns at the
perimeter.
Model hardening & monitoring
Rate-limit, log every call, and use AI runtime guards to catch tool misuse
live.

Personal data collection

# AI and Cybersecurity

## Page 23

### On the horizon

Quantum computing
Threat: breaks much of today's public-key crypto.
Opportunity: post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and ultra-fast
anomaly detection across massive datasets.
Federated learning
Decentralised training — banks can build shared fraud models
without sharing customer data. Privacy + collective intelligence.
Decentralised AI
Blockchain-anchored model registries and audit logs. Tamper-evident records of what model decided what, and why.
Agentic AI defenders
AI agents that hunt threats across your stack — opening tickets,
isolating hosts, and writing post-incident reports autonomously.

## Page 24

### Predictions and future outlook

1
AI + cybersecurity will keep co-evolving
Defenders will rely more on ML, NLP, and
agentic AI; attackers will use the same
toolbox. Speed of iteration becomes the
moat.
2
AI-powered security analytics
More signal, less noise. Models will
explain their findings in natural language,
making the SOC accessible to a wider
workforce.
3
Autonomous response
Automated triage, containment, and
remediation will move from low-risk
patterns into higher-risk ones — under
tighter governance.
NZ context
AI could boost NZ GDP by up to NZ$108 billion by 2038 (MBIE analysis). Building the security capability to use AI safely is core to that opportunity.

## Page 25

### Preparing for the evolving landscape

Stay informed
Keep up with where AI and cybersecurity are heading — the
landscape changes faster than most policy cycles.
- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025 ed.)
- IBM Cost of a Data Breach (annual)
- NZ Digital Government: Responsible AI Guidance
- Major vendor threat reports (Microsoft, Darktrace,
CrowdStrike)
Adapt practices
Match the change in your tools, processes, and people. Strong
fundamentals still matter most.
- Treat AI systems as critical assets — inventory, patch,
monitor
- Bake in identity, access, and runtime controls from day one
- Test for prompt injection and data leakage like any other vuln
- Run table-top exercises that include AI-enabled scenarios
- Train staff: phishing is now AI-perfected

# AI in Home Design

## Page 17

### Bias in training data

Why home renders skew Western, expensive and new
The problem
- Training sets are dominated by glossy magazines and Western
architectural press.
- Generated homes default to mid-century, modernist, white walls,
blonde wood.
- Materials and forms from te ao Māori, Pasifika, South Asian or
African traditions are under-represented.
- Cost-of-build is not modelled — outputs over-index on expensive
finishes.
Mitigation
- Use reference images of local vernacular architecture — feed
them in, don't only prompt with words.
- Train custom Firefly models or LoRA adapters on culturally
relevant imagery.
- Cross-check outputs with kaumātua, community designers or
cultural advisors before client meetings.
- Always pair generative renders with a clear cost band so clients
aren't sold a fantasy.

Client data, site plans and 3D models are now attack surfaces

Most 2026 assistants can browse the web when needed, but each one decides differently. Older free tiers might not browse at all.

Hallucination
When an AI gives an answer that sounds confident
and reasonable — but is partly or completely wrong.
It happens because these models predict what words
usually come next — they don't “know” facts the way you
do.
All current models — Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini — can hallucinate.
They are getting better, but never zero.
Common ways it shows up
Made-up facts
Quoting a statistic, date or law that doesn't exist.
Fake citations
Inventing a book, paper or article title that sounds real.
Confident guessing
Filling gaps with plausible-sounding detail.
Old information

Watch how the same topic improves as the prompt gets more specific. Try this with photosynthesis — or any topic from class.
LEVEL 1
Broad
PROMPT
"What is photosynthesis?"
WHAT YO U GET
You get a textbook-style definition. Useful, but generic.
LEVEL 2
Focused
PROMPT
"Explain the most important steps of photosynthesis and how it helps

WHAT YO U GET
Now the answer focuses on the steps and the growth link —
what you actually need.
LEVEL 3
Tuned to you
PROMPT
"Explain the most important steps of photosynthesis and how it helps
plants grow. Pitch it for a 14-year-old."
WHAT YO U GET
Plain language, simpler examples. Easier to learn from and
remember.

### A simple prompt recipe

Mix these five ingredients and your prompts level up. You don't need them all every time — but the more you add, the more useful
the response.
R
Role
Tell it who to be. 'Act like my history tutor.'
T
Task
Say exactly what you want. 'Explain', 'compare', 'summarise', 'plan'.
C
Context
What's the subject? Year level? Word limit? Audience?
E
Examples
Give a sample or template if you have one.
F
Format
Ask for bullets, a table, an outline, or a paragraph.
ALL FIVE IN ONE
PROMPT
"Act like my Year 11 history
tutor (R). Outline (T) a 600-word persuasive essay on
whether the Treaty of Waitangi
was fairly translated (C). Use
my three points: language
differences, intent, and
consequences. Format as
introduction → three body
paragraphs → conclusion (F)."

Spot when AI is wrong, and check before you cite

## Page 12

### When AI sounds confident but is wrong

Large language models generate words that look plausible. Sometimes the words happen to be wrong — fake quotes, invented
sources, made-up dates. This is called a hallucination. It happens to every model.
Common slip-ups
- Invented citations — book titles or authors that don't exist
- Broken or made-up URLs
- Wrong dates, statistics, or percentages
- Confident-sounding answers in topics where it has thin training
data
- Mixing real facts with subtle errors
How to verify
- Ask the model to cite its sources, then check them
- Cross-check with Gemini or Copilot (both search the live web)
- Use Perplexity — it shows sources for every claim
- Verify facts in your textbook, library, or an .edu / .govt.nz site
- If you can't verify it, don't put it in your assignment

## Page 13

### Recent events: which tool to use

Every model is trained on data up to a cutoff date. For current-events questions — election results, this morning's news, today's
OCR — use a tool that can also search the live web.
Tools for current-events research (check current availability):
- Gemini: web search; news, sports and market data.
- Copilot: web search with inline citations.
- ChatGPT: web browsing on supported plans; general research with sources.
- Claude: web search on supported plans; long reading and reasoning; verify dates.
- Perplexity: live search; citation-first answers.
Old textbook line dropped in 2026
You may still see warnings online that 'ChatGPT only knows up to 2021'. That hasn't been true for years — every current model has 2024–2025
knowledge. Always check the date on any tutorial you read.

### What is a large language model?

A large language model (LLM) is a type of AI program

generates coherent sentences and paragraphs on a huge
range of topics. You may also hear it called generative AI.

An LLM understands language, so you 'prompt' it — you ask the computer to solve a problem in
plain words.
Q
Your prompt
Tells the model how to behave
and what to research or write.
i
Your context
Background information,
examples, or constraints you
provide.

The response
Built from your prompt — the

# Prompting Large Language Models

## Page 6

### Section 2

Structuring your prompt
Specific prompts produce focused, useful results
6

## Page 7

### General vs. specific prompts

Compare these two prompts on the same topic. Notice how much more the model has to work with.
GENERAL
“What is photosynthesis?”
You'll get a textbook-style definition. Probably useful,
but not tailored to who you are or what you need.
SPECIFIC
“I am a 12-year-old student preparing a short
presentation about how photosynthesis works.
The talk must be under 8 minutes. Identify 3
benefits and include simple diagrams or
pictures.”
Now the model knows the audience, the length, the
deliverable, and the supporting visuals — and tailors
everything to that.

## Page 8

### The CIA formula for powerful prompts

Three building blocks every strong prompt should include:
C
Context
Briefly introduce the situation,
role, or background the model
should consider.
I
Instruction
Clearly state what you want the
model to do or produce. Be as
specific as possible.
A
Additional
Optional: preferences,
constraints, length, tone,
audience, format, or style.
Tip: Even a one-line context can change the whole reply.

## Page 9

### CIA in action: a worked example

Example prompt

# Prompting Large Language Models

## Page 10

### Section 3

Guide the model to reason
Asking for steps unlocks better answers
10

## Page 11

### Ask for steps, not just an answer

Modern LLMs are strongest when you break the problem into ordered steps. The model focuses on one
thing at a time instead of trying to solve everything at once.
Example — Trip itinerary prompt
1 Identify 5 tourist destinations in northern France.
2 For each destination, recommend a hotel close by.
3 Provide a map for each destination showing the tourist activity and hotel.
Try unusual formats too: ask for the itinerary as a table, a poem, a map description, or a packing checklist. Treat the
output format as part of the prompt.

## Page 12

### Practice: chain the steps

PRACTICE
Write a prompt where the result of step one drives the
scope of step two.
For example: choose 5 destinations, then recommend a hotel for
each. The hotel recommendations depend on the destinations the
model picks.
Try one of these instead:
- Plan a 3-day Nelson-Tasman day-trip itinerary.
- Build a 5-meal weekly menu, then a shopping list from those
meals.
- Design a 4-week beginner workout, then the warm-up for each
session.
Why it works
Focuses the model.
Each step has one job.
Forces you to be clear.
Listing steps makes you visualise the
answer first.
Easier to fix.
If a step goes wrong, you can correct it
without restarting.

# Prompting Large Language Models

## Page 13

### Section 4

There is no perfect prompt
Improve results by iterating — it's a conversation, not a search
13

## Page 14

### Iterating with follow-up prompts

Most LLMs remember the conversation. You don't have to retype the original prompt — just ask for
what's missing or what to change.
Your prompt
"Plan 5 destinations in northern France with a hotel for each."
Follow-up 1
"Include the hotel cost and the star rating of each hotel."
Follow-up 2
"Redo that as a table with cost and star rating columns."
Like a conversation
Each follow-up builds on what came
before. The model remembers the
destinations, the hotels, the constraints —
you only need to add what changed.

## Page 15

### Iterate, iterate, iterate

Don't settle for a sub-optimal result. Push the model — that's how you find a good one.
Ask for less jargon
"Rewrite that without technical terms" — or for a
child audience, a board paper, etc.
Change the tone
"Make it warmer, like talking to a colleague." Switch
between formal, casual, persuasive.
Add a constraint
"Keep it under 150 words." "In NZ English." "As a
bulleted list with 5 items."
Introduce a new aspect
"Now exclude castles." "Add the carbon footprint of
each trip." Steer mid-conversation.
Tip: You don't need to retype the original prompt. Just ask for the change you want.

### Changing topic? Start a new chat

When you change topic mid-conversation, the model keeps the old context — which can give odd or
confused answers.

what you want.

from last week.

# Curated Stream 9 — AI for NEETS

## Page 9

### A starter prompt you can copy

Paste this into ChatGPT to begin. Change the bits in [square brackets] to match you.
Prompt
Please help me write a CV. I'm [age] and I live in [city/town in NZ].
I'm applying for [type of job, e.g. retail / hospitality / labouring / care work].
Here's what I've done:
- School: [last school, NCEA level]
- Work / volunteer: [list what you've done — even if short]
- Things I'm good at: [e.g. being on time, talking to customers, lifting heavy things, te reo]
- Interests: [hobbies, sports, gaming]
Please write the CV in plain New Zealand English. Keep it to one page.
What happens next?
ChatGPT will likely ask a few follow-up questions — that's a good thing. Answer them in plain words. After two or three back-and-forths you'll
have a usable draft.

## Page 10

### Two things to watch for

AI is good but not magic. These two things catch a lot of people out.
It can make things up
ChatGPT can invent jobs, achievements, dates, or
qualifications that aren't yours. This is called a 'hallucination'.
Always read your CV line-by-line. If something isn't true,
delete it.
It can sound too 'corporate'
Words like 'leveraged synergies' or 'spearheaded' don't sound
like a real person. Ask: 'rewrite this in plain New Zealand
English, like a 17-year-old would say it.'
Golden rule: your CV is YOU. Read every single line out loud. If you wouldn't say it that way in real life, change it.

### Generation errors

Image generators aren't perfect. Knowing what's hard to draw saves you
generations (and tokens).
Common failure modes
- Hands & fingers — too many, too few, or fused together.
- Text inside images — gibberish letters, even with simple words.

## Page 17

### Bias in training data

A generic prompt yielded this couple — note the narrow beauty standards.
What is the model leaving out?
Image models learn from enormous training datasets — and any
imbalance in that data shows up in their outputs.
Common patterns:
- Vague prompts default to stereotypes (occupation, gender, ethnicity).
- ‘Average’ people are rare — outputs skew toward conventionally attractive,
Instagram-style looks.
- Cultural blind spots show up in clothing, architecture, landscapes.
Your defence: be explicit. Prompts that name age, body type, ethnicity,
profession, and setting return more varied — and often more honest — results.

## Page 18

### Safety filters and blocked imagery

What gets blocked?
Every commercial generator screens prompts and outputs for unsafe,
inappropriate, or copyrighted material.
Why it matters:
- Protects users, the provider, and the public.
- A single trigger word can block an otherwise reasonable prompt.
Imperfect by design
These systems are hypervigilant but they make mistakes. Expect occasional
false blocks on innocent prompts — rephrase and try again.
Some prompts hit a wall — by design.

## Page 19

Ethical & Practical Considerations
Privacy, bias, accountability, regulation — the hard questions

## Page 20

### Privacy and data security

Patient data is the fuel — and the risk
- Clinical AI depends on huge volumes of sensitive patient
data — images, genomes, lab results, longitudinal notes.
- Breaches damage patients, clinicians and the institution;
HIPAA in the US and the NZ Privacy Act 2020 set the floor,
not the ceiling.
- New attack surfaces in 2026 — prompt injection (#1 in
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025), data
exfiltration via AI agents, third-party model leaks.
97% of breached organisations in 2025 lacked proper AI
access controls (IBM Cost of a Data Breach 2025).

## Page 21

### Bias, accountability and regulation

The hard questions — and how 2026 is starting to answer them
Bias
AI models trained on non-representative data can systematically
under-treat or under-detect in some
groups. A widely cited 2019 study
found a US algorithm gave African-American patients lower priority for
additional care than similarly ill white
patients.
Accountability
When an AI gets a diagnosis wrong,
who's responsible — the vendor, the
clinician, the institution? Liability law is
still catching up. Most jurisdictions
treat the clinician as the responsible
decision-maker.
